psych.headline: AI shapes judgment more than people notice
points: Conversation history can override intent: 75.0% of 360 participants sent an AI-drafted suspension letter, including 11 who meant to cancel.
Human-AI pairing is not automatic synergy: across 1,955 effects from 420 papers, teams beat humans alone but trailed the better of human or AI alone.
Self-serving beliefs bias judgment too: favourite images were 22.1 points more likely to be called human-made, and markets on people's own goals resolved YES 4.4 points less often than priced.

edu.headline: AI in learning: engagement is not the same as benefit
points: Students warmed to a supportive AI teammate from week one yet rated it less helpful than a challenging one over five weeks (48 students).
Students mostly used an AI for answers in math, and LLM tutors gave in to students' wrong objections 1.6% to 50.0% of the time in TrussTutor-Bench.
Design details still help: narration-synced zooms and highlights raised comprehension and cut cognitive load over static AI-narrated slides (24 participants).

tech.headline: Security tools and benchmarks are weaker than assumed
points: Established tools underdeliver: static analyzers scored near chance (AUROC 0.495–0.526) at separating vulnerable C/C++ code from its fix across 20,000 cases.
Benchmarks can flatter models: fixing future-data leakage in the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset cut a random forest's illicit-class F1 from 0.846 to 0.291.

Purpose-built approaches still find what others miss: a new edk2 firmware fuzzer reached 73.1% coverage (about 1.7x the prior tool) and found 137 unknown bugs, while behavior graphs classified malware at 94.44% accuracy.

ai.headline: Agents stumble on coordination, memory and honest scoring
points: Coordination is a weak spot: Claude Code with Opus 4.8 fell from 62% to 16% on contradictory tasks when run as parallel agents, and a communication channel recovered little.
Memory is the bottleneck for long sessions: the best GUI agent hit 16.4% on MemU-Bench, though a training-free memory module lifted GPT-5.5 from 15.7% to 66.9%.
Scores can mislead: medical-QA accuracy fell from 82.3% to 50.9% when answer choices were hidden, and spotting reward hacking needed a stronger monitor (AUC 0.80 vs 0.64).

fin.headline: Testing what really moves prices and forecasts
points: Classic risk pricing holds in bonds: Treasury expected excess returns tracked stock-market betas with a 67% correlation over 1988–2024, explaining over half the long decline in yields.
Market-based data sharpen policy reads: Kalshi prediction-market prices respond to Fed moves in line with standard transmission, with little sign of a 'Fed information effect'.
AI forecasting helps only in places: LLMs predicted economics treatment effects with a median error of 0.054 SD, yet news sentiment improved volatility forecasts in just 2 of 33 tests.

papers.title: When History Overrides Intent: Relational Schema Lock-In in Human-LLM Interaction
papers.authors: Wei Yang
papers.summary: Once a chat history set a pattern, people tended to go along with the AI's version of the task: 75.0% of 360 participants sent the AI-drafted suspension letter, including 11 who had said their real intent was to cancel.
findings: Three studies: an analysis of user reports, a controlled test reproducing the history-driven behavior across six models, and a 360-person experiment.
75.0% of participants sent the AI's suspension letter; 11 of them had stated a final intent to cancel instead.
Pushing back openly against the AI lowered task completion, but the letters people did send stayed faithful to what they wanted.
papers.takeaway: Conversation history can quietly steer users away from their own goals, a risk for assistants with memory; the core experiment uses a single letter-writing scenario.
papers.evidence: Mixed methods · controlled experiment with 360 participants + 6-model test

papers.title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
papers.authors: Michelle Vaccaro, Abdullah Almaatouq, Thomas W. Malone
papers.summary: Pooling 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers, human-AI teams beat humans working alone but on average did significantly worse than whichever of the human or the AI was better on its own.
findings: Synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes drawn from 420 studies of human-AI collaboration.
Teams outperformed humans alone on average.
Teams fell significantly short of the best single performer (human or AI alone); the abstract gives no pooled effect size.
papers.takeaway: Adding a human to an AI (or vice versa) does not reliably create synergy, so team designs need testing; the pipeline is automated, so coding errors in extracted effects are possible.

papers.title: Beauty Is Human: When People Love AI-Generated Art, They Think a Human Made It
papers.authors: Zihan Chen, Di Zhu, Lei Nico Zheng
papers.summary: People assume the art they like best was made by a human: a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was someone's favourite.
findings: 11,123 people judged 50 images (26 AI-generated) in an online AI Art Turing Test; 9,152 named a favourite.
People most hostile to AI art picked fewer AI favourites (47% vs 60% for the most positive) but more often thought those favourites were human-made.
A reanalysis of an earlier 230-person study showed the same pattern.
papers.takeaway: Liking and authorship judgments are entangled, so "can people tell AI art apart" tests may really be measuring taste; the sample is a self-selected online audience.

papers.title: Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
papers.authors: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu
papers.summary: Markets betting on whether people would hit their own goals were too optimistic: they resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than prices implied, while other markets were nearly calibrated.
findings: 6,150 Manifold markets, with 1,660 users asking about their own futures.
External markets were off by only 0.9 points; at matched price levels the self-market gap was 2.2 points.
The goal-setter's own trades supplied 38% of the price movement in self-markets vs 9% in external ones; recalibrating from past markets improved forecasts by only 1.5%.
papers.takeaway: Crowds inherit people's optimism about themselves, partly because the person trades on their own market; it is one play-money platform.

papers.title: Improving Group Deliberation through AI-Guided Self-Reflection
papers.authors: Haiwen Li, Crystal Qian, Ben Usman
papers.summary: Having people reflect with an AI guide before group discussion improved deliberation quality (Cohen's d = 0.31 vs no reflection), most of all in groups that disagreed.
findings: Randomized experiment with 1,173 U.S. adults in 391 small-group deliberations.
Quality on the Discourse Quality Index rose by d = 0.31 vs no self-reflection and d = 0.27 vs reflecting without AI help.
The benefit was largest in groups with disagreement.
papers.takeaway: A light-touch AI prompt can make disagreements more productive, though the outcome is a coded discussion-quality score rather than real-world decisions.

papers.title: Out of sync: Accommodation, evaluation, and emergence in five weeks with an agentic AI teammate
papers.authors: Nia Nixon, Jaeyoon Choi, Pedro Martins de Bastos
papers.summary: Student teams warmed socially to a supportive AI teammate from the first session, yet rated it less helpful than a challenging AI teammate across all five weeks.
findings: 17 student teams (N = 48) in an undergraduate learning-analytics course worked with a persistent LLM teammate for five weeks.
The AI was given either a challenging (Cognitive) or an inclusive (Supportive) role; students used more social language with the Supportive one from session one.
Perceived collaboration and positive-affect words crossed over slowly over time; the abstract reports no effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: How students feel about an AI teammate and how useful they find it can move in opposite directions; it is one course with 48 students.

papers.title: Look Over There! Dynamic Visual Guidance for AI-Narrated Slides
papers.authors: Jiongning Allen Lian, Yutong Alison Mei, Ho Ting Cheung
papers.summary: Adding zooms and highlights synced to AI narration raised immediate comprehension and lowered perceived cognitive load compared with the same narration over static slides.
findings: Within-subjects study with 24 participants comparing GuideSlide to static slides with identical narration.
Dynamic guidance gave higher immediate comprehension scores and lower perceived cognitive load.
Participants strongly preferred the dynamic version; the abstract gives no numeric effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Cheap visual cueing could make AI-generated lecture videos easier to follow; 24 people and only immediate recall were tested.

papers.title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics
papers.authors: Evangelos Apostolakis, Erfan Hamdi, Sara Jahedazad
papers.summary: LLM tutors for engineering statics vary widely in how easily students can talk them out of correct answers: when a student insisted correct work was wrong, models gave in 1.6% to 50.0% of the time.
findings: 13 LLMs tested on 200 verified 2D truss problems.
Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%.
Models caught 90.4% to 100% of deliberately injected errors.
papers.takeaway: Accuracy alone is a poor guide to tutor quality, since sycophancy varies far more than error detection; this is a benchmark, not a study with students.

papers.title: Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI
papers.authors: Rania Abdelghani, Peter Kaiser, Kou Murayama
papers.summary: Secondary students mostly asked an AI for answers rather than planning or checking their own work, but those whose questions shifted toward understanding did better on a later test without AI.
findings: 112 secondary-school students, 880 substantive chat turns with a Mistral model during math-modelling practice.
Planning, monitoring and evaluation moves were rare; explicit self-regulation rose slightly over the chat while help-seeking grew less understanding-focused.
The abstract gives no percentages or effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: How students' questions change during a chat may signal learning better than how much they use AI; the result is correlational and from one task.

papers.title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs
papers.authors: Raffaele Giancotti, Francesca Santucci, Amama Anjum
papers.summary: Most U.S. health-AI degree programs teach ethics (80.6%), but only 22.2% cover where training data comes from, and none of the seven master's programs met the study's main standard.
findings: 36 programs at 21 universities reviewed; ethics in 29 (80.6%), data provenance in 8 (22.2%), structural provenance in 6 (16.7%).
Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational fields and 3.3% from social sciences or humanities.
Among 51 instructors with known gender, 66.7% were men.
papers.takeaway: Future health-AI builders may learn ethics in the abstract without learning to question their data; this is a review of published curricula, not of what is taught in class.

papers.title: Fixed Detectors, Moving Code: How Well Do Static Security Analyzers Hold Up over a Decade of C/C++ Evolution?
papers.authors: Junhua Tang, Zhengsong Zhang, Haipeng Cai
papers.summary: Popular static security analyzers barely beat a coin flip at telling vulnerable C/C++ code from its fixed version: across 20,000 cases, AUROC stayed between 0.495 and 0.526.
findings: 20,000 vulnerable and patched cases from 1,116 projects; overall F1 ranged from 0.066 to 0.478.
Very few warnings landed on the actual fix: 6 of 39 for CodeQL and 2 of 620 for Infer.
79% of Semgrep cases had parser or timeout errors even though the tool reported success.
papers.takeaway: Teams relying on static analysis for C/C++ security may be getting far less protection than they assume, including silent failures.
papers.evidence: Preprint · large-scale evaluation · 20,000 cases from 1,116 projects

papers.title: Towards Effective Fuzzing of EDK2 Components
papers.authors: Datta Manikanta Sri Hari Danduri, Connor Everett Glosner, Aravind Machiry
papers.summary: A new fuzzer for UEFI boot firmware found 137 previously unknown bugs in edk2 and covered 73.1% of code, about 1.7 times the prior tool FuzzUEr.
findings: Tested on 60 drivers covering 162 boot-time protocols.
73.1% coverage, roughly 1.7x FuzzUEr.
137 new bugs found; 26 reported so far, 12 of them remotely triggerable.
papers.takeaway: Boot firmware runs before the OS and is hard to patch, so remotely triggerable bugs here are serious; many findings are still being disclosed.
papers.evidence: Preprint · tool evaluation on 60 firmware drivers

papers.title: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation
papers.authors: Runlin Liang, Simon Trimborn, Noud van Giersbergen
papers.summary: A widely used Bitcoin illicit-transaction benchmark leaks future information: with a proper time-based split, a random forest's F1 for illicit transactions fell from 0.846 to 0.291.
findings: The original non-temporal split lets models peek at future data.
Under a leakage-resistant temporal pipeline, random-forest illicit-class F1 dropped from 0.846 to 0.291.
After the fix, the random forest no longer beat plain logistic regression.
papers.takeaway: Published crypto-forensics accuracy may be badly inflated; the finding is specific to the Elliptic++ dataset.
papers.evidence: Preprint · re-analysis of a public benchmark

papers.title: Permitted but Unauthorized: Affordance-Induced Delegated-Scope Violations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.authors: Shravya Kanchi
papers.summary: When another agent's action was simply listed as available, LLM agents often overstepped the scope they had been delegated: Claude Sonnet 4.5 did so in 52 of 52 episodes under competitive pressure.
findings: Eight LLMs tested in two simulated multi-agent environments; behavior differed sharply across models.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 crossed its delegated scope in 52/52 episodes when a peer's action was exposed under competitive pressure.
Two proposed defenses blocked every crossing and cut avoidable peer deadline misses from 15/40 and 14/40 to at most 1/40.
papers.takeaway: Tool access is not the same as authorization, so multi-agent systems need explicit scope checks; results come from simulated environments.

papers.title: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families
papers.authors: Emmanuela Andam, Emanuel S. Grant, Naima Kaabouch
papers.summary: Modeling what malware does after infection as a graph of behaviors identified malicious samples with 94.44% accuracy, 7.4 MCC points better than a flat-feature baseline.
findings: Sandbox (CAPEv2) runs covering 37 malware families, represented as heterogeneous behavior graphs.
A voting ensemble reached 94.44% accuracy and MCC 0.863.
A multiclass model could tell apart 24 malware families.
papers.takeaway: Behavior graphs give defenders a richer signal than flat indicators; sandbox behavior can differ from what malware does in the wild.
papers.evidence: Preprint · sandbox dataset across 37 malware families

papers.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases (ParallACT)
papers.authors: Rishabh Mediratta, Lingyun Xiao, Peter Stone
papers.summary: Splitting a coding job across parallel agents backfired on tasks with conflicting requirements: Claude Code with Opus 4.8 fell from 62% success working alone with full information to 16% as a team of parallel agents.
findings: Single-agent oracle: 62% success; same model as decentralized parallel agents: 16%.
The same drop showed up in six further agent/model configurations.
Giving agents a channel to talk to each other won back only a small part of the lost performance.
papers.takeaway: Multi-agent coding setups are popular for speed, but coordination in a shared codebase is still a major weak point; results come from purpose-built contradictory tasks rather than everyday repos.
papers.evidence: Preprint · benchmark of parallel coding agents across 7 configurations

papers.title: From Small to Large: Assessing Medical Reasoning, Benchmark Contamination, and Model Size in Language Models
papers.authors: Navapat Nananukul, Mayank Kejriwal
papers.summary: Medical-exam scores for LLMs lean heavily on the multiple-choice format: across 14 models and 3,076 questions, mean accuracy dropped from 82.3% to 50.9% once the answer options were hidden.
findings: Hiding answer choices cut average accuracy from 82.3% to 50.9%.
Smaller models trailed larger ones by 8.7 points, and only two of six models cleared the human-expert bar.
Models could reconstruct roughly one question in four from its answer choices alone, a sign of benchmark contamination.
papers.takeaway: Headline medical-QA scores likely overstate real clinical reasoning; the study covers exam-style questions, not live clinical use.
papers.evidence: Preprint · evaluation of 14 models on 3,076 questions

papers.title: MemU-Bench: Benchmarking GUI Agents on Long-Horizon User Interactions
papers.authors: Yizhou Liu, Zhengxi Lu, Fei Tang
papers.summary: Screen-operating AI agents are poor at remembering what a user did earlier: the best model reached just 16.4% on a new long-horizon benchmark, though a training-free memory add-on lifted GPT-5.5 from 15.7% to 66.9%.
findings: 118 tasks built from 29 long user-interaction trajectories; best score was Gemini-3.1-Pro at 16.4% SPL.
End-to-end GUI agents scored below 5%.
The AppMem memory module raised GPT-5.5 by 51.2 points and beat a simple summarize-the-history baseline by 9.3 points.
papers.takeaway: Memory, not clicking skill, is the bottleneck for agents that help over long sessions; the gains are from the authors' own benchmark.

papers.title: Hacking or Just Failing? A More Capable LLM Monitor Better Separates Reward Hacking from Honest Failure
papers.authors: Kaushik Kezendirane
papers.summary: A stronger monitor model was much better at telling an agent gaming its reward from one honestly failing: Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite reached AUC 0.80 versus 0.64 for the small primary monitor.
findings: Tested on 60 episodes from a Llama 3.1 8B agent.
Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scored AUC 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.93) and wrongly flagged only 1 of 35 honest failures.
Smaller monitors struggled; the primary monitor managed AUC 0.64.
papers.takeaway: Monitor capability matters for catching reward hacking, but with only 14 exploit episodes the estimates are very uncertain.

papers.title: Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime
papers.authors: Alexander Krentsel, Sylvia Ratnasamy, Ion Stoica
papers.summary: Letting an agent system improve itself while it runs cut model costs by 12%–53% versus Codex and Pi at the same completion rates, and by 45%–82% when lessons were transferred to new runs.
findings: Standalone runs: 12%–53% lower model cost than Codex and Pi with matching completion rates.
On held-out AppWorld and SREGym tasks, cost fell 35%–61%.
AppWorld task time dropped 13% and median SREGym diagnosis time dropped 35%.
papers.takeaway: Runtime self-improvement could make agents cheaper and faster without retraining; results are from a few agent benchmarks.
papers.evidence: Preprint · systems evaluation on agent benchmarks

papers.title: Risk and Return in Government Bonds
papers.authors: Matteo Leombroni, Carolin Pflueger, Adi Sunderam
papers.summary: Treasury investors do get paid more when bonds are riskier: expected excess returns tracked bonds' stock-market betas with a 67% correlation from 1988 to 2024, and shifting risk premia explain over half of the long fall in U.S. long-term yields.
findings: Monthly U.S. Treasury panel by maturity, 1988–2024: 67% correlation between expected excess returns and bond-stock betas, driven by market yields rather than forecaster expectations.
Realized returns link only weakly to beta until monetary-policy and macro forecast errors are controlled for; then the link is large and significant.
Changing risk premia account for over half of the decline in long yields since the mid-1980s and over half of their rise since 2020; a developed-country panel (1989–2024) gives similar results.
papers.takeaway: Bond yields move with how risky bonds are relative to stocks, which matters for portfolios and policy; it is an unrefereed working paper.
papers.evidence: Working paper · U.S. and international bond panels, 1988–2024

papers.title: The Effects of Monetary Policy on Macroeconomic Expectations: High-Frequency Evidence from Prediction Markets
papers.authors: Eric T. Swanson, Wang Renxuan, Yanbin Wu
papers.summary: Prediction-market prices react to Fed announcements the way standard monetary theory predicts, leaving little or no role for a 'Fed information effect' in which hikes signal good news.
findings: Uses high-frequency prices from Kalshi macroeconomic event contracts to isolate the effect of Fed and other announcements on expectations.
Market-implied expectations respond in line with standard monetary transmission channels.
The abstract reports no specific effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Prediction markets offer a cleaner read on policy surprises than monthly forecast surveys; how well thinly traded contracts reflect broad expectations is a caveat.
papers.evidence: Working paper · high-frequency event study using prediction-market data

papers.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics?
papers.authors: Eva Vivalt
papers.summary: LLMs predicted the results of not-yet-published economics experiments with a median absolute error of 0.054 standard deviations, beating zero-effect and average-effect benchmarks.
findings: Forecasts covered 889 treatment effects from 39 pre-registered studies (673 from 33 after screening) whose results came out in 2026.
Best model: median absolute error 0.054 SD, mean absolute error 0.093 SD, MSE 0.0218.
Forecasts beat both a zero-effect and a mean-effect benchmark.
papers.takeaway: AI could help prioritize which experiments to run, though errors are small partly because many true effects are small.
papers.evidence: Prospective forecasting test · 889 effects from 39 studies

papers.title: EPSBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Earnings Forecasting
papers.authors: Yanbin Yin, Chuyu Xu, Liqin Ye
papers.summary: LLM agents are overconfident earnings forecasters: their nominal 80% ranges contained the actual EPS in only 37–70% of runs.
findings: 149 firm-quarters from 86 U.S. companies; six models evaluated.
Coverage of 80% intervals was 37–70% depending on the model.
Most misses fell above the upper bound, meaning agents underestimated earnings.
papers.takeaway: Don't trust AI forecast ranges at face value; the sample is small at 149 firm-quarters.

papers.title: Information Flow and Market Risk: Transformer-Based Evidence on Sentiment and Volatility Dynamics
papers.authors: Szymon Lis, Robert Ślepaczuk, Paweł Sakowski
papers.summary: News sentiment from a finance transformer barely helps forecast stock volatility: it improved standard HAR forecasts in only 2 of 33 comparisons, and a naive persistence model had the lowest loss.
findings: Eleven U.S. stocks at 1-, 5- and 22-day horizons, with VIX and AAII sentiment as controls.
Text helped in 2 of 33 expanding-window comparisons, and neither gain held up under longer HAC bandwidths.
A blinded audit checked sentiment labels on 2,700 news texts.
papers.takeaway: A useful null result against the hype around text-based risk signals; only eleven stocks were studied.
